author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Detect thermal throttling during long PS2 sessions
summary: Correlate a gradual speed decline with elapsed heat, thermal status, and controlled changes such as lower resolution or removing an insulating case, while avoiding unsafe cooling and misleading scene changes.
heroAlt: Official PCSX2 power-performance settings screen representing controlled power-policy testing

blocks.text: Distinguish elapsed heat from a heavy scene

Thermal throttling commonly appears as acceptable cool-start performance followed by a gradual decline that persists across scenes. A single difficult boss or effects-heavy room creates a workload-local drop instead. Use a route that revisits the same checkpoint at several elapsed times and record Android thermal status where the device exposes it.
Stop on a system thermal warning, painful surface temperature, swelling, moisture, or unstable charging. Do not place the phone in a freezer or use condensation-prone cooling.

items: A repeatable checkpoint visited at cool, middle, and late times.
Stable ambient conditions and documented case use.
One battery range with charging disabled for the baseline.
Thermal status or temperature trend from a trustworthy system interface.
An alternate profile with one lower GPU-cost setting.

blocks.text: Correlate speed with temperature and a controlled relief

items: 1. Begin from a documented cool idle state and cold-boot the baseline profile.
2. Record speed and thermal status at the checkpoint before extended play.
3. Follow the fixed route and revisit the same checkpoint at regular intervals.
4. Mark when speed first declines and whether clocks or thermal status change at the same time.
5. Stop safely, cool back to baseline, and repeat with one lower internal-resolution step.
6. On a separate run, remove an insulating case only if device handling remains safe.
7. Compare the time-to-decline rather than only peak FPS.
8. Choose a profile with reserve before the system reaches severe thermal status.

blocks.text: A lower GPU workload or improved passive heat path that delays the same decline supports a thermal diagnosis. It does not prove exact silicon temperature because many consumer readings are partial or filtered. The repeated checkpoint keeps scene complexity constant while elapsed heat changes.
Classify throttling only when heat and performance move together repeatedly.

items: The same checkpoint slows as the session warms.
Thermal status or clock trend changes near the decline.
Cooling to baseline restores the earlier behavior.
A lower-cost profile delays or reduces the loss.
No unsafe warning or moisture occurs during testing.
One scene is always slow from a cool boot: diagnose its workload.
Stutter follows storage reads rather than elapsed time: test I/O separately.
Battery saver activates at the same charge threshold: isolate power policy.
Charging heat exists only when plugged in: compare charging as a separate condition.

blocks.text: Return the case, display brightness, and per-game profile to the accepted daily configuration. Remove experimental monitoring overlays and let the device cool naturally before normal charging or another run.
Surface temperature is not junction temperature

A cool case does not guarantee the SoC is cool, and a warm surface can reflect effective heat transfer. Use performance curves and system thermal status together rather than a single touch judgment. Compare the timestamp of the first sustained speed decline with clocks, temperature state, battery current, and surface conditions. A repeatable downward curve after warm-up is stronger evidence than one isolated hitch, while a sudden drop at the same game event should be investigated as workload before it is labeled thermal throttling.
